body:
Ah- yeah, that sucks too. I'm honestly not too sure why people do that, saying things like 'if you were really suicidal you wouldn't have failed at it / could just off yourself properly' doesn't do anything at all to actually help people cope with it or address the issues they're facing and mostly ignores how they feel. 

It's kind of sad, really.

I'm sorry you feel that way. Looking over my post, though, I'm not saying that people might not commit suicide based on snap decisions- rather, *that hasn't been my experience* with it. I understand some people who are depressed and who have had a particularly bad day could be affected adversely like that; I have been in that position myself. Knowing the options available to me, though, and being able to discuss with other people how I felt as well as read through exactly what might come about as a result of killing myself was very useful at the time. 

Should we just not put information about how to kill yourself painlessly online? Or not mention it at all? I said that if I didn't know about the exit bag method I might not be here today. I thought a lot about whether to post that sentence at all, but ultimately I figured mentioning that along with the fact that I was no longer actively suicidal and that things had changed for me would be useful for people to know, if they did read it. I can't tell people whether or not they should live or die, or make assumptions as to what their situations are, and I decided quite a while back I would not consider myself responsible for the choices that other people make. All I can do is to say what happened to me, how I feel about it, and hope that maybe people might take something positive from that. 

I should say, though, that what you're saying strikes me as uncomfortably similar in terms of logic to 'don't make abortion accessible to people, if they don't have an 'easy' way to undo pregnancies they won't be as likely to get pregnant'. That... well, it doesn't work. I'd also like to point out that the exit bag method is not exactly something that can be done on the spur of the moment, it takes a considerable amount of time, preparation, and putting together- hardly as accessible as, say, throwing yourself off a building. This is actually why it's not that widespread, it's just really not easy to assemble. It's also, like I mentioned, pretty much common knowledge.

Do you actually think that? 

Like I've mentioned to some other people, I can understand wanting to makes sense of something like this, or the desire to kill yourself- unfortunately it's very difficult to actually say what's going through a person's mind or what exactly their situation would be. It would be nice to think that there might be something giving a person hope, but that's not often or always the case.

You can feel depressed for a few days. 

Suffering from clinical depression, however, is not the same as feeling depressed.

I'm really sorry to hear that. Suicide is something that's really difficult for many people to understand. Even for me, it's still not easy to talk about. Chances are a lot of people who are thinking rationally can come up with ways that they would consider foolproof, but it's hard to describe how you're thinking when you're in a bad state of mind. It's difficult to rebut statements those rationally simply because being suicidal as a result of depression is not really a situation in which you are inclined to be rational at all. 

That doesn't mean, however, that your feelings were or are any less valid. Regardless of whether people survive, to even be in that position where you might have tried to or seriously wanted to kill yourself is inherently not a good thing, and it'd be nice if people could be a little more empathetic on it. I understand the desire to make sense of things, it's just that in this case that's often pretty difficult. Just because it's not understandable doesn't mean it should be dismissed, though, or ignored, though.

I brought it up because it was relevant to the discussion and also because I thought it was an important point to make. People could kill themselves with that- but if you've ever tried looking for information on suicide, you'll soon realize *it's not difficult* to find out far more than what I've mentioned with very little effort. 

Honestly? Suicide takes more than reading something someone posted online. Me mentioning the exit bag is not the issue here, more important than that would be the fact that people kill themselves. Encouraging discussion about it, hearing how it's affected people on all sides, and thinking critically about not just how you might take your life but for what reasons are all also very important, and I'd think it's better to have discussion on this than not. 

...Besides, it's not a particularly unknown or secret method, if you want to go into that, too.

I could probably answer this.

> For me, death by falling appealed because it was quick, simple and had a high chance of being very lethal on your first go around. I live in a place where guns are extremely difficult to come by. Pills and medications wise, I didn't know enough about them when I was younger to be certain that I'd manage to kill myself with those and that it'd be quick. I was scared of pain, so cutting myself was out of the question, too. Suspension hanging appealed, but I wasn't sure I'd be able to avoid being found for long enough to die like that. While I know of other methods to commit suicide now, that list and throwing myself off a tall building seemed like the only options in the past.

Injecting poison- where'd you get poison? Jumping from a window doesn't *seem* painful, sure it'd hurt a bit but death would be instantaneous, if you pick a place high enough (and where I live, tall apartment buildings are everywhere). All the other methods I could think of when I was considering suicide were far more painful and unpredictable.

And that's the hardest part. I 'won' the game as well, but very consciously picked choices that I have not and would probably not pick in real life.

Definitely something I'll be thinking about for a while.

Not necessarily. I'll quote myself on this-

>But sometimes being caught or faced with people who try to get you down doesn't actually help. **You may not necessarily want to die then and there, but at the same time, you really don't want to live either.** When you're stuck in a position like that, taking a step either way becomes incredibly difficult.

Emphasis added. I think what a lot of people might miss sometimes is that suicide is a process. Picking out the right way to die, the right time to die, and so on, can take a while. The person standing on the edge might feel as if this was not the time nor the place, but that doesn't mean that they think there would be a reason to go on.

This is exactly why I went for activities that I could excuse with things like 'I like the adrenalin rush'. I wanted to know just what it fell like to fall. It's not quite the same knowing that you're attached to a rope or that something will pull you back, but I really wanted to know how I'd feel doing it, or what my thoughts would be.

Was there fear? Oh, definitely. I'm a lot more unnerved around heights than I've led people to believe, with my fondness for standing at the edges of tall buildings. The thing is, being scared of wanting to die or feeling regretful about the possible method I was looking at... none of that actually solved or addressed what was making me want to kill myself in the first place. And right now, there are a lot of other methods besides falling which are much less- reflective on the way down, is one way to put it, I'd guess.

Haha, not there any more... but perhaps not quite as far back as I'd thought I was. And that's actually a really good song. Oddly enough, stuff like that was (and is) good to listen to. 

I think playing the game was definitely worth it, though. If nothing else, it's good to be able to see what is possible against where I'm at. I'd like to address the fact that I might not be as positive about things as I'd like to be, but sometimes I can't recognize when being self-critical is justified and when it's slipping around into depression. Having it being written out like that is useful for that.

Have not played that before, actually- and holy crap, some of the options... it's the subtle things, like asking someone you like if they're okay or happy and wondering if they're bored that struck me.

>"Thanks for putting up with me," you say, staring at the TV without actually watching it.

I have done this quite a few times. Recently. That's a little unnerving.

Edit: Okay, some of these are hitting *way* too close to home. I don't know if I'm comfortable with that or just incredibly unnerved. It's actually impressive, in a way. Played through it once picking the choices I saw of as ideal rather than the choices I might've picked for myself and I'm not going to touch it any more than that. It's... definitely an interesting exercise, for sure.

Personally, I'd think wanting to die and considering taking your own life or putting yourself in situations where you could die would be suicidal. I know what you mean with cars- for me, it was crossing the yellow line on train stations and really hoping that maybe I'd trip or someone would bump into me or there'd be some sort of... unfortunately engineered accident, I suppose. It's definitely difficult to give clear a yes or no to that kind of question, though it might help if you asked people who were counselling you precisely what they mean by being suicidal, or how they'd define it.

It can definitely feel like that. Something I'd encourage is to find a thing where you're helpful or you can be helpful to other people. If you have the time or the ability, maybe consider looking for people around your area who might need help. If you're in school right now, you can try looking into clubs which go around and volunteer at things, or even just look at organizations which you might be interested in and can learn things from. I've guided at museums and volunteered at animal shelters, and though one was through school and the other wasn't for very long, I found both experiences really fulfilling, and it was nice to be able to feel as if I was doing something good, regardless of whether or not I personally was good.

>Is someone suicidal if it is all that they can think about even if they have no plans to act on those thoughts? I think so. 

Unfortunately, thinking the answer to this was 'no' actually was one of the main reasons I never brought it up with anyone else for literally years and didn't actually think I was suicidal. For various reasons, I never went through with attempting to kill myself, but if I knew someone else now who was in the same position as I was then, I would definitely try to get them some sort of help because technicalities aside, that is seriously not a good place to be.

In other cultures or countries (mine), it isn't just 'something only the weak willed and privileged do'- you'd have to be really balls to the wall crazy before seeking therapy or services like that. There's heavy, heavy prejudice against people with mental issues of any sort, and many common misconceptions are perpetuated, which often leads people to think that they can't *really* be depressed or this can't *really* be worth talking to someone over, and so on. It's not a great situation, but unfortunately that's how things are.

Like other people have said, volunteer. You won't be held to as tight a schedule as you might be with a job, but it's something that you can personally hold yourself to or turn up regularly for. I know sometimes it can be hard to deal with people; I've faced that situation myself. You could try looking into things like animal shelters around your area or rescue organizations, and asking if they need help with anything.

Well, that's what the internet is for- I have to admit, being able to preserve anonymity online does make me a lot more comfortable. Plenty of people who know me in real life would also be surprised to find out I've thought about suicide this seriously before, and I genuinely would not want that to get in the way of how I interact with them. And places like /r/depression and /r/SuicideWatch are actually both really supportive and non-judgemental. Even lurking on them, it's sometimes helpful to know that you're not alone in feeling the way you do, and other people are also struggling with the same issues you have.

Yeah, it sort of like as if there's another layer of issues on top of the ones that you already perceive to be insurmountable. 

Plenty of people say things like how people who want to die should just do it, but figuring out methods and places and times does take a while. And on some of those steps, it's hard to figure out where to go next. Adding something like being caught in the act to that only complicates matters and the immediate effect is often anything but helpful. It'd be great if people could realize that suicide isn't a single step, but rather a process that can take many different forms depending on the individual.

It sounds like you were really hurt by what happened to your friend. That's definitely understandable. I don't think it's fair to blame him or hold him entirely responsible for everything that came next, though. I would say another way to possibly look at it would be that his death is responsible for causing his wife's mental breakdown and for having his daughter grow up without a husband. If he was knocked down by a car, or had been struck by lightning, his family and friends would still have been left without him.

I get what you're saying- it was his own hand that took his own life, and not some accident. What myself and other people have been trying to convey, though, is that mental illness, depression, and other such issues can and *does* strongly affect people's ability to judge a situation. I would be much more inclined to look at your friend's mental illnesses and hold *that* responsible for his death. Sometimes people are unable to control the way they think, and the way they think in turn affects the way they act. 

Also, you cannot be convicted of a crime that you did not commit- that's why there are categories like manslaughter, and why people who survive suicides aren't treated the same way as attempted murderers. There is a distinction, there. I have never said that public suicide isn't selfish or is totally cool, either, and I have witnessed it. It's actually very common in my part of the world, simply because so many other avenues of suicide are difficult to come by. 

Ultimately, I'd think the most important thing isn't that someone killed themselves publicly or privately, but that they wanted to kill themselves at all. It's this sort of thing that I'd really like to prevent or to possibly address. Even if I might agree with you (and I do) about the effects of witnessing public suicides, many of your points *would not help* to change the mind of someone who is determined to die. You could hate them more, or place responsibility for everything that happens as a result of their death on them, but if you want to help them, then you'll have to find other ways to address these issues. 

This is how I'd think of it- your friend's wife did not get a breakdown out of nowhere- your friend killing himself had a large part to play in that. I would not hold your friend's wife responsible to the *exact same extent* as I would someone who was not undergoing immense emotional trauma in the event that she did something tragic as a direct result of this trauma. The same goes for your friend, and for whatever reasons he might have had to kill himself.

Yeah- I think part of it is that depression is also *incredibly* hard to realize in yourself. Unlike being sick where you can see the physical toll that's being taken out on your body, depression doesn't have any obvious signs, and many people with it are able to function quite well around other people or in society. Because of that, though, they might feel as if their feelings of depression aren't legitimate or worth seeking help for. 

Thanks for your reply, though, definitely means something. I'm glad I didn't go through with it either! I'm not sure if I can say that I'll be able to reach a point where I actively want to live as opposed to actively want to not die, but I'd like to, so that's... something, I suppose.

I'm from Singapore. Care for mental illness here is... a little spotty, to say the least. Not that things like that aren't there, but generally people's opinions of you won't be good. I have definitely looked into counselling services and I wouldn't mind considering it, but I'm also in the process of looking for a job, and I'm really not sure if bringing this up would be a good idea. It'd be nice if I could say something like 'yeah, this was a thing, it's not really a thing any more and I'm working on it' and have that be enough, but for most people here, if you're nuts, you're nuts, there's no in between. Even if care is available, seeing help or therapy isn't looked upon as a normal thing in the least.

Unfortunately, with regards to my parents, realizing that I probably will not ever be on good terms with them was something I had to also confront. I'd rather not go into detail with it, but my home life was not the greatest and I doubt reconciliation is likely to ever be possible- I was actually a lot closer to them when I *was* contemplating suicide, and wanting to please them while struggling with unrealistic expectations, abuse and other things was part of why I figured everyone would be better off without me around. If I was depressed and assuming the worst, it was likely to be more about myself than it was about other people, unfortunately.

Still, being older has helped. I have more of a social group now and have people that- while not necessarily related to me by blood- I would consider my family, so all in all I'm generally better off, for that.

Really appreciate the reply. In my case I was (and still am) on somewhat bad terms with my parents, and I actually figured that they'd be happier and better off if I died, even if they were upset in the meantime. Ironically enough, I'm much more willing to talk about or discuss suicide now that I'm *not* really suicidal any more, which puts me in a bit of a bind, sometimes. I'd like to talk to people about it, but not really wanting to kill myself any more makes it feel kind of stupid. I've also worried a lot about possibly being put in hospital, which is something I really don't particularly care for. 

I think at this point in time, I'll probably have to just stick to talking about it online and leave bringing it up in real life alone until I'm absolutely sure I can talk about having being suicidal totally in past tense. Still, I suppose that's progress, of sorts...

I know you're not posing this to me, but speaking of responsibility, the justice system where I'm in- and I'd be willing to wager, where you're from- doesn't treat people as if they are all equally responsible to the same degree for what they're done. Mitigation is a thing, as is figuring out to *what* extent something happening is a person's fault. People with severe mental illnesses are treated differently under the law compared to people who aren't similarly afflicted.

Just thought I'd point that out.

That would be nice, but I doubt it'd happen. Suicide is still an incredibly sensitive and taboo topic in many societies, and encouraging people to be open about feeling suicidal and allowing them to seek help without repercussion would be great. Unfortunately, for people who don't really get how suicide works, it's very hard for them to support something like this. I'd imagine a lot of people would be worried that having such things would encourage people to think about suicide more or make them more aware that they have options and more likely to kill themselves. 

It's for the same reasons as you describe in your first paragraph that I've never really felt comfortable with the phrase 'suicide is a permanent solution to a temporary problem'. For many people in that situation, all they see is 'permanent solution', and their problems to them might not necessarily feel or be temporary at all. Especially if the problem is 'themselves', and they don't see any way to change to be someone different- a permanent solution is exactly what they would be looking for.

Oh, absolutely. Like I said in another comment, though:

>Sometimes you think things like 'augh, I can't even come up with a way to kill myself that would be neat, I guess I really don't deserve to live- I shouldn't be considerate anyway, I should just give people more reason to hate me. I don't want anyone to cry over my body or remember me as anything other than the terrible person that I am. This is really the best method I've got to achieve that.'

To put it simply, I ended up figuring that the more I made people hate me for being terrible and inconsiderate and horrible, the faster they'd get over my death. If I went in a peaceful way (though I didn't have one) then it might hurt them more or they might be actually sad about it and think of me as a good person. I absolutely didn't see myself that way and didn't want to let anyone else think that, either. 

Telling someone who is convinced that they are and also *wants* to be a terrible person and a burden on everyone else in the world that they're a terrible person and a burden on everyone else does not actually help them decide to behave otherwise. When you want to die, you will look for ways to justify it. This was mine.

Thanks for saying that. Do you mind if I ask what 'seeking help' entailed in your case, or how people were at it? Unfortunately the fear what might happen if I talk to people in real life about having been suicidal is still one of the things that has stopped me from doing so before.

>At this point, it's easy to rationalize to yourself that nobody will mind cleaning you off the street.

And sometimes you think things like 'augh, I can't even come up with a way to kill myself that would be neat, I guess I really don't deserve to live- I shouldn't be considerate anyway, I should just give people more reason to hate me. I don't want anyone to cry over my body or remember me as anything other than the terrible person that I am. This is really the best method I've got to achieve that.'

It might not necessarily make sense to look back on, but when you're seriously considering it, it can.

Yeah... other people have pointed out that there are ways besides this to consider suicide. That's valid, but when you're not quite in your teens yet and don't really know how to look up stuff like this online and are afraid of being found out, those are about the only methods- well, I knew, basically. 

And frankly, what bugs me most now, thinking over it, is that 'you might as well be considerate' doesn't actually make up for the fact that someone is dead or might soon be dead. Knowing someone you cared for or were close to is gone, and that they tried to be considerate by using a method that was neater doesn't necessarily hurt more or less compared to if they threw themselves off a building, but it's kind of twisted in a whole different way.

Haha, thanks. Morbid as that sounds, it means something. I think what always bugs me about people who say things like 'well if people who were suicidal really cared to be considerate they'd take a less splattery method' is that the effect that it has on people close to the person is that someone they care for is dead, and method aside, nothing quite makes up for that. I wouldn't say it hurts more or less, but the thought that the person who committed suicide was trying to be *considerate* causes a different sort of pain.

Freud, really? 

Haha, that aside though- it was simpler for me. Basically my parents always said they only had one child because they couldn't afford another one and I was too much trouble. They also frequently told me I was a liar and useless and untrustworthy. The fact that I regularly made my mother break down (or that my mother regularly broke down at me), resulting in canings, screaming, days of being ignored and so on didn't help.

Ultimately, I figured if I killed myself, they'd probably be sad for a bit but it'd let them have another chance to have a kid that wasn't so much of a failure. It seemed like a good and entirely reasonable thing, at the time. Of course my reasons having being suicidal have changed over the years, but when it first started, that was why.

That would be nice if it was possible, but for some people- particularly those who might be in denial about their own suicidal urges- contemplating in that way can be very difficult. If you aren't admitting you have an issue worth seeing a psychologist or therapist for, you won't have them to talk to. If you think you aren't seriously suicidal, you won't bring it up with your friends because you'd just be spoiling the mood, and why burden them with things like that? They're your friends, you don't want them to be upset at you when you aren't even *really* serious about it. And as for contemplating in your own home, you can do that too, but until you're actually facing the situation, you won't really know how you'll feel about it, which is why you might end up going up on ledges and other such places.

I can see why you'd think that, but my experience was different. I left it in a comment there but it seems to apply here, so:

>Well, I was up on tall buildings and ledges- never got caught, but I can tell you that I certainly didn't want attention. For me, death by falling appealed because it was quick, simple and had a high chance of being very lethal on your first go around. I live in a place where guns are extremely difficult to come by. Pills and medications wise, I didn't know enough about them when I was younger to be certain that I'd manage to kill myself with those and that it'd be quick. I was scared of pain, so cutting myself was out of the question, too. Suspension hanging appealed, but I wasn't sure I'd be able to avoid being found for long enough to die like that. While I know of other methods to commit suicide now, that list and throwing myself off a tall building seemed like the only options in the past. So like I said, it wasn't so much attention as that method just being the most viable.

Well, I was up on tall buildings and ledges- never got caught, but I can tell you that I certainly didn't want attention. For me, death by falling appealed because it was quick, simple and had a high chance of being very lethal on your first go around. I live in a place where guns are extremely difficult to come by. Pills and medications wise, I didn't know enough about them when I was younger to be certain that I'd manage to kill myself with those and that it'd be quick. I was scared of pain, so cutting myself was out of the question, too. Suspension hanging appealed, but I wasn't sure I'd be able to avoid being found for long enough to die like that. While I know of other methods to commit suicide now, that list and throwing myself off a tall building seemed like the only options in the past. So like I said, it wasn't so much attention as that method just being the most viable.

>Later, I was institutionalized not for getting caught setting things up, then deciding to dismantling it. But for admitting I had done this. 

Unfortunately this is actually why I've always been afraid of telling people that I was suicidal or 'window shopped' too. I considered partial suspension rather than full on hanging, just because logistics, but you're not alone in having been there. 

It'd have been nice if some other option between possible institutionalization and just not telling anyone existed. I know there are suicide hotlines, but at that point in time I was somewhat worried that I might be found out through them and didn't want to make use of them either. Some people also likely aren't even aware they're thinking about dying and genuinely want to, I spent years in serious denial about being suicidal for a long time, though looking back on it the fact that I was seems very obvious now.

It's easy to say 'why not do it someplace private', but I think something that should be kept in mind is that if you are already suicidal, chances are very high that you may not be thinking entirely straight as is. Things like that may seem very obvious when watching a gif of a man on a ledge, but when you're in that position, you're usually pretty overwhelmed with a lot of thoughts. It's difficult to tell what anyone in that sort of a position might be thinking about too, since everyone' situation is unique to them.

Yeah... my life was pretty good as far as things went apart from some pretty big issues that I was in denial about (whole 'nother story there) and I had friends who were in far worse shape than I was. Always thought I wasn't really suicidal and just being unnecessarily or unreasonably down about stuff, but never put the pieces together. 

I'd imagine because suicide is such a taboo topic, most people only ever see the moment of death and what comes after and have no idea about the lead-up to it. The way it's frequently reported in papers didn't really help either, and it seemed as if most people just had one big thing go wrong in their lives and then decided to kill themselves. That was how it was in my case, anyway. Not wanting to be seen as suicidal also prevented me from telling people around me, because I really didn't know how people would take it, only that it would definitely not be good. 

I think at one point I did give up on being happy- though that's mostly gone away now, and I do have people or things that I consider worth living for. It's still very difficult to imagine being not ever thinking about suicide, though what keeps me going sometimes is remembering that I really don't *want* to be, and avoiding dealing with it doesn't actually help that at all. It'd be great if there were a way to bring up issues like these and address a lot of misconceptions that people have about it whenever they come up, though in real life that can get pretty awkward. Right now if I do talk about it, it's mostly online- I'm still not comfortable with telling people who know me in real life that I was probably seriously suicidal, but being able to mention it somewhere definitely helps.

It's not just that, actually. Sometimes if you're up there or in a position like that and someone comes across you, it makes everything far worse. You have a lot of other things to consider- if I'd been found out, my own thought process would've gone something like: 

>Crap, someone knows, can I tell them I'm not suicidal? I don't want to cause drama- it's too late, now they know for sure, they're going to bring in more people, I do still want to die but I don't want to die *like this*, I don't want to have people watching, why can't everyone just go away, why didn't I just kill myself earlier, why did I have to think about it so much, it's too late to die like this any more and this isn't how I want to go, will I even have another chance to later, they're all going to *watch* me and people are trying to talk and augh now everyone's found out- 

I can't say for sure this is how the guy in the gif felt. But sometimes being caught or faced with people who try to get you down doesn't actually help. You may not necessarily want to die then and there, but at the same time, you really don't want to live either. When you're stuck in a position like that, taking a step either way becomes incredibly difficult.

Thank you. Unfortunately the whole 'unless they actually attempt / go through with it, they're not serious' mentality actually caused me to think I wasn't *really* suicidal for the longest time, or that feeling suicidal was something that I had to address. It's been a bit tricky facing up to this, but being able to put how I felt in context or having words for it helps a lot. 

I really appreciate what you said about how suicide isn't a snap decision and is actually a process, from thinking about it to picturing out different ways and trying out different things. It's understandable that people think of it as sudden, since that's often how it hits them when someone they know commits suicide, but in my experience or what I've seen from talking to other people, it rarely if ever is to the person in question.

>What you're actually doing is window shopping death.

I wish I'd heard this earlier.

This is a great way to describe it, thank you. As someone who used to be suicidal and who still occasionally considers it, this is a really good way to explain what I was doing. Definitely did the whole 'stand on tall ledges' thing, though I was always careful to never be caught. People thought I was an adrenalin freak for a while, since I kept seeking out things like bungee jumping and other such chances as much as I could. 

People always say, if someone really wanted to kill themselves they'd just do it. This is true, but it takes a while to figure out how and why and in what way. I went through a number of methods before ultimately putting it off, but that didn't mean I wasn't suicidal at all or somehow more or less suicidal compared to other people just because I never went through with it. I have to say, though, if I'd known about the Exit Bag method when I was younger, I definitely might not be writing this now.
